style: calm, natural hesitations, like explaining to a friend
slides: The third way to find arguments: points of view.
We look at the issue from one direction, then another, then another. Social-economic, psychological, educational, moral, and more.
So, the third way: points of view. We take a step back and look at the issue from above, like we did when we analysed the task. But now, through nine points of view.
A lot of students call them different fields, or angles, or aspects. The social aspect, the economic aspect, and so on.
Here's the list I work with. Nine points of view.
Social-economic. Psychological. Educational. Moral. Democracy. Rights. Safety. Environment. And science, medicine and progress.
And for each one, we ask, from this point of view, how does the decision affect things? Now, not every point of view fits every task. That's fine. We check them all, and keep what works.
What this does is, it opens up your mind. Just by making yourself think in different directions, you'll find way more arguments than you expected.
For each point of view, there's one question to ask yourself.
Social-economic: how is money involved here? Psychological: how does it affect the way people feel and behave? Educational: what does it teach?
Moral: is it fair? Democracy: how does it affect majority rule and representation? Rights: which rights are involved, and is the harm proportionate?
Safety, environment, and science, medicine and progress: how does it affect people's safety, nature, and health and technology?
You'll find this list in the card after this lesson.

The first point of view is social-economic. Let's start with the economic half. Well, what can you do, money is almost always one of the things to consider. In the end, someone has to pay. So where does the money come from? Who pays, who loses, who gains?
It's a point you can fit into almost every task. Let's take a few examples. Reduced tax for large companies.
If large companies pay reduced tax, the state gets less tax. Less money comes into the state.
But on the other hand, the people who start working in these companies will earn more money.

And there's also a third side. If the state gets less from taxes, someone has to pay. The state budget doesn't come out of nowhere. If these companies don't pay, the money comes from the ordinary citizen.

And you can look at the long term. In the short term, the state gets less tax money. In the long term, it may actually make it stronger. More people work, there's less unemployment, and that makes the economy stronger.
Another point is the companies themselves. They'll earn more. Now, I'm not sure we'd choose to use that argument, but in some cases, maybe. So it's important to be aware of it.
Now let's take the face-recognition camera task.
I can say, wait, you need to set up this whole network. Building it and running it costs a huge amount of money. Someone has to pay. So where will it come from?
And I can argue that it comes on top of the bodies we already have today. Even if the cameras are running, you still need the police officers. Someone to go and catch, someone to go and search.

And from the other side, someone can argue, wait, this network will actually save money. With the cameras, we can catch offenders faster, and spend fewer resources searching for them and finding them.
We have evidence that they're guilty. Once we've caught them, that's it, they go to prison. No need to let them go and chase them again, and waste more and more resources.
So to sum up, money is connected to almost everything. You'll find it very easy to bring in. But you need to practise. It won't just jump out at you.
Now, the social half of social-economic. Because we don't live in a vacuum. We live in a society, and there's almost always some effect on society.
For example, reduced tax for large companies. The companies start hiring people, so there are fewer unemployed. And that helps make society stronger.
Or face-recognition cameras. Maybe they'll make people go out less, into public spaces. They care about their privacy. They don't want to be followed.
So there are fewer social interactions. The whole way people meet and connect could change. Suddenly people start meeting only in private homes, and they don't go out.
So it's clear there's a social effect. And from here, I can take it in all kinds of directions.
The next point of view is educational. And I don't mean tasks that are about education, like home schooling, rewarding students, or how to pay teachers.
I mean the effects on education. On how a child is brought up. Not necessarily learning. Through all kinds of things we do.

For example, if there are face-recognition cameras in public spaces, what does that say? We're teaching our kids not to trust. Not to trust each other. Maybe to be afraid of the street. There have to be cameras, because the street is so dangerous.

And from the other side, someone could argue exactly the opposite. I'm teaching them not to be afraid in the street. Don't worry, everything's filmed, everything's fine. Either way, it has an educational effect.

And by the way, educational effects aren't only on kids. A lot of the time the argument is, I want to educate the population to do certain things. Not through enforcement or laws, but through education.
For example, the pension law. We have to put money aside for a pension. In the past, whoever wanted to did it, and whoever didn't want to, didn't.

Some said, let's pass a law that makes people save for when they stop working. Others said, no. If you want people to look after their financial future, educate them. Give them courses on financial planning. But don't force them. It's their money.
Now, the point of view I love the most. The psychological one.
Why? Well, one, we can bring it into almost anything. Because almost every action or decision has psychological effects on people. Or could have.
Examples from our tasks. Reduced tax for large companies: unemployed people start working. And that has a huge effect on them. Suddenly they feel they're worth something.

People who've been looking for work for a long time often become depressed, impatient, and stressed. It affects their whole life. So when you give someone a job, and let them make a living with dignity and support their family, it has an enormous effect.
Face-recognition cameras: people start to feel they're being followed. Their behaviour becomes paranoid. Wait, am I being filmed here? Or not?
Besides the fact that it fits almost every task, the main reason I love it is that not many students use it.

And if I use arguments that aren't common, the rater says, wow, I've got someone with nice critical thinking here. The economic argument? Yes, yes, everyone writes to me about money. But psychological? Nice angle.

And that shows in the score. Let's say a psychological argument, which isn't so common, affects the rater psychologically. He gives me a bit more credit for how original my argument is... even if I supported it exactly as well as others support other arguments.
Let's go quickly through the rest of the list. One short example each.
Moral: is it right? Is it fair? Is it fair that the richest companies pay less tax than the corner shop?
Democracy: who has the power, and who controls it? A camera network built to fight crime could one day be used to follow journalists, opponents, or demonstrators.
Safety: people's physical safety. Cameras could stop an offence while it's happening, or help find a missing child within minutes.

Rights: which rights are involved, and is the harm to them proportionate? Anti-smoking laws, for example. The smoker's freedom, against the non-smoker's right to health. There's a whole lesson on this soon.
Environment: land, pollution, natural resources. A reduced tax brings new factories. Jobs, yes. But also pollution, and open land that's gone.

Science and progress: tax big companies to protect small shops, and people stop buying the cheapest, most efficient product. Then there's less reason to invent the next cheaper, better thing. So it's a question about taxes... and the argument is about progress.
Not all nine will fit every task. Go through them anyway. It takes a minute, and the one you almost skipped is often the original argument.
I'll end this lesson with a recommendation.

I meet a lot of students who have the list of fields. Sometimes they make acronyms. Sometimes they use the ministers method, the minister of economy, the minister of finance, the minister of education. That's how they try to remember it.
But just knowing the fields doesn't help you find the argument. To find arguments, you need to think. It's not enough that I tell you, social. Okay, wait... I don't know how it affects anything.
You need to practise. You need to try it. Write the eight practice tasks at the end of this course. And look at lots more tasks.
There are dozens of NITE tasks that have already been published. Go through them, analyse them, and try to find arguments.
And you don't always have to write the whole essay. You can just go through a task and see if you manage to find arguments. Practise this part.
Now, one more thing. Some students mix up rights with points of view. For example, a social right, like the right to education, and the educational point of view.
The right to a proper education is my right. It's something I'm entitled to get. In this case, from the state.
In the educational point of view, I ask myself, what effect does this have on education? What effect does what we do, or choosing this position or that one, have on how kids and adults are educated?
So that's the third way: points of view. Go through all nine, one direction at a time. Next, we'll see all nine in action on one task, and then take a closer look at rights.
